video_title: How North Korea Stole $6.3 Billion From Binance Without a Private Key
gist: Laura Shin, Jonty (founder of a threat-intelligence firm) and Pablo Sabatella (founder of OBSAC) dissect North Korea's ~$6.3-6.4B hack of Binance hot wallets on Oct 29: no private keys were leaked; attackers compromised internal signing infrastructure (starting from a DevOps laptop) and used EIP-7702 delegation to sweep EVM wallets. Roughly 43% (~$3B) was frozen by Tether, Circle and the Arbitrum Security Council, and the guests argue opsec (EDR, threat understanding) and industry refusal to enable laundering venues like THORChain are the real fixes.

themes.theme: Attack mechanics: signing infra, not keys

insights.claim: Binance's ~$6.3-6.4B hot-wallet drain across Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron, Solana, XRP and multiple L2s was achieved without stealing private keys; attackers got Binance's internal signing infrastructure to sign malicious withdrawals.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Key-custody hardening alone does not protect exchanges if the systems that instruct signers are compromised.
insights.quote: The fact that this affected so many different wallets on different chains um is is like clearly indicative that that it's the infrastructure that's been compromised.

insights.claim: Binance likely uses HSMs, but an HSM that trusts whatever an internal server tells it can be abused by simply hacking that server, making the keys irrelevant.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Exchange security audits should focus on the authorization layer feeding HSMs, not just the HSMs.
insights.quote: you don't need the keys and you need to tell that tell uh the HSM to do whatever you want to do.

insights.claim: The attacker pre-signed 50 transactions with different nonces so one would land right after a legitimate withdrawal; that transaction used EIP-7702 to upgrade the hot wallet into a smart account controlled by an attacker contract, which then swept all assets, including new deposits arriving mid-attack.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Delegation features let a single malicious signature convert a wallet into an ongoing drain.

insights.claim: EIP-7702 was not the root vulnerability; the hack would have happened without it, but it made the drain faster and is heavily used by drainer kits, and every new feature enlarges attack surface.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella and Jonty
insights.so_what: Expect debate over 7702 risk, but the policy lesson is opsec, not protocol rollback.
insights.quote: this hack would have happened with or without 7702. It just made it slightly faster.

insights.claim: Nine out of ten big crypto attacks in the last three years started with an infected employee laptop.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Endpoint security is the highest-leverage control for crypto firms.
insights.quote: nine out of 10 attacks of the big attacks that happened, all of them start with a laptop being infected

insights.claim: Binance's initial attribution to a single compromised DevOps engineer laptop was walked back a day later when 'additional points of breach' were found, suggesting the initial tweet was preemptive.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin / Jonty
insights.so_what: Early exchange incident statements are unreliable; wait for full post-mortems before judging control failures.

insights.claim: Pablo believes initial access came via a developer laptop followed by lateral movement and privilege escalation inside Binance, and that a transparent post-mortem will show initial compromise occurred at least many weeks before the theft.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Dwell time is long; detection windows for exchanges should be measured in weeks/months.
insights.quote: we will see in the end that this initial access was at least many weeks ago.

insights.claim: Organizations should assume at least one device, account, key, server or API key is already compromised and design compartmentalization around that assumption.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Assume-breach architecture is the baseline for custodians.
insights.quote: We have to assume that at least one of our devices is compromised.

insights.claim: Holding over $6B in hot wallets is not necessarily a security failure for Binance, because a bank run at its scale could require servicing more than $6B in withdrawals quickly, and the funds appear spread across multiple keys.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Hot-wallet size criticism is weaker here than in the Bybit case.

insights.claim: A security researcher (Andrew Mohawk) spotted what appears to be test transactions for this attack mechanism on October 8, three weeks before the hack, and the attacker also tested with Tornado Cash-funded wallets on the day.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella / Laura Shin
insights.so_what: Pre-attack on-chain tests mainly widen forensic windows rather than enabling prevention.

insights.claim: Pre-hack test transactions have limited preventive value because they reveal the mechanism but not the target; their main use is for incident responders to extend log-review windows.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Don't rely on on-chain early-warning as a defense strategy.
insights.quote: we shouldn't be relying on on on that as a as a way forward to protect ourselves

themes.theme: Escalating DPRK threat and copycat hacks

insights.claim: Binance's ~$6.3B loss is the largest hack in history, compared with North Korea's estimated annual GDP of about $26B.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: A single theft equal to roughly a quarter of DPRK GDP makes crypto a core state funding channel.
insights.quote: North Korea's annual GDP is estimated to be about $26 billion.

insights.claim: Per Chainalysis, suspected North Korea-linked hacks account for nearly 89% of reported crypto hack losses this year, up from 15% in 2021, and average loss per DPRK hack rose from $50M in 2021 to $185M in 2026.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (citing Chainalysis)
insights.so_what: DPRK is now the dominant crypto counterparty risk and is getting more effective.

insights.claim: Within days of the Binance hack, Mercado Bitcoin in Brazil was hacked for $40M and an unnamed EU entity for about $100M, and Pablo expects things to get far worse because AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Expect a continued wave of large exchange hacks; security spend and insurance costs should rise.
insights.quote: I really believe things are gonna get far worse than this.

insights.claim: After this hack, North Korea holds more ETH than the Ethereum Foundation.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: A state adversary is now a major ETH holder, a potential overhang as it liquidates.
insights.quote: now DPRK holds more ETH than the EF.

insights.claim: 'Lazarus' is now a catch-all; North Korea's Reconnaissance General Bureau has pivoted large parts of its workforce to crypto theft, splitting into sub-units like TraderTraitor, AppleJeus, Contagious Interview and Dangerous Password with distinct TTPs.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Defenses should be tailored to specific DPRK units' tradecraft.

insights.claim: TraderTraitor is the most prolific DPRK crypto unit, responsible for the Binance, Bitget, LayerZero and Bybit hacks; it typically compromises developers via multi-round fake job interviews with a coding test that runs trojanized code on corporate laptops.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Hiring-process lures targeting devs are the key initial-access vector to defend.

insights.claim: The industry's understanding of how North Korea operates does not match the threat it poses; firms that don't understand DPRK units should learn or hire someone who does.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Threat-intel capability is an underpriced need for crypto firms.

insights.claim: Notification work among trusted contacts foils many more DPRK attempts than are publicly visible, but better notification is not the highest-leverage fix; operational security is.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Prioritize internal opsec spend over relying on external alerts.

insights.claim: About 43% of the stolen funds (~$3B) were frozen by Tether, Circle, Ripple and the Arbitrum Security Council, versus less than 3% frozen in the initial aftermath of the Bybit hack, which is unprecedented.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Industry freeze capacity has materially improved, reducing net attacker proceeds.
insights.quote: I think it's like 43% of the funds being stolen is completely unprecedented

insights.claim: Circle and Tether froze quickly this time largely because the hack hit their own bottom line through partner Binance, unlike Drift, where Circle was criticized for not acting.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Stablecoin issuer freezes are driven by commercial incentives, not consistent policy.
insights.quote: this hack affects everybody's bottom line. There is huge huge incentive for these companies to step in and freeze the funds.

insights.claim: Faster freezes will not change North Korea's macro behavior of stealing whatever it can, but will change early laundering; after the LayerZero incident TraderTraitor began moving funds off Arbitrum almost faster than it swaps out of USDC.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Expect attackers to prioritize exiting freezable venues/assets first.

insights.claim: Laundering at a $6B scale breaks DeFi liquidity: some swaps lost up to 10%, one swapped $5M for $72 on a thin DEX, and MEV searchers, builders and platforms like THORChain captured roughly $50M from the laundering flows.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella / Jonty
insights.so_what: Mega-hacks create slippage windfalls for MEV searchers and stress DeFi venues.

insights.claim: The attacker sold ~$60M of USDT to market makers and borrowed just under 20,000 ETH against stolen collateral on Aave, echoing the Kelp DAO hack; Aave froze markets across all networks in response.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin (host)
insights.so_what: Lending protocols are a channel to convert freezable assets into unfreezable ETH, creating bad-debt and contagion risk.

insights.claim: With billions still left to launder, the attacker may repeat the bad-collateral borrowing tactic on other lending protocols, raising DeFi-wide questions in coming months.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Lending protocols face elevated near-term risk of stolen-collateral borrowing.
insights.quote: There's still billions of dollars left to launder.

insights.claim: DeFi protocols will need circuit breakers that pause when very large amounts move, though attackers (especially with AI) could split transactions under thresholds.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella / Laura Shin
insights.so_what: Expect circuit-breaker features to spread across DeFi protocols.

insights.claim: Arkham's claim that the Binance hacker deposited $4M to Binance is a mischaracterization: funds were swapped on THORChain and Arkham traced through Asgard vaults to arbitrageurs who use Binance for liquidity.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Binance may face pressure to cut liquidity to THORChain arbitrageurs.

insights.claim: The chaotic fan-out of funds to hundreds of addresses is likely done by Chinese-speaking money-laundering organizations, not DPRK itself, using scripts to defeat attribution/taint-based monitoring by Chainalysis, TRM and Elliptic; AI makes this easier at scale.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Taint-based compliance tooling is being deliberately gamed by scripted peel chains.

insights.claim: During TraderTraitor hacks (Bybit, LayerZero, Bitget, WazirX), 99%+ of THORChain's volume on those days is laundering for North Korea, and probably the majority of its all-time volume.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: THORChain fee revenue spikes are a direct function of DPRK laundering, a major regulatory risk.

insights.claim: THORChain halted signing on many chains after an Ethereum reorg caused a 10 ETH shortfall; only three node votes were needed for the emergency halt, and the protocol has stayed halted for days, so restarting means node operators knowingly reopen a DPRK laundering channel.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin / Jonty
insights.so_what: THORChain governance is concentrated and operators face personal legal exposure on restart.

insights.claim: THORChain is not meaningfully decentralized: node operators follow leaders like Chad Barraford and JP Thor in a herd, dissenting operators left, and new node operators cannot join without approval.
insights.speaker: Jonty and Pablo Sabatella
insights.so_what: The 'decentralized' defense against regulators is weak for THORChain.
insights.quote: If you want to put a fortune a fortune node, you cannot do it without their approval first.

insights.claim: THORChain founders are being sued in New York over the THORFi incident and are defending by arguing the protocol's admin keys were always centralized, contradicting years of public decentralization claims.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Litigation record undermines THORChain's decentralization narrative.

insights.claim: The FBI, Secret Service and IRS-CI explicitly named THORChain node operators among parties asked to block TraderTraitor-linked transactions, which the guests see as a clear warning shot.
insights.speaker: Laura Shin / Jonty
insights.so_what: Elevated odds of US enforcement action against THORChain participants.
insights.quote: I think if you're being named in an FBI press release as one of the enablers who could help launder the funds from literally the biggest hack ever.

insights.claim: Tornado Cash differs from THORChain because Tornado runs on immutable contracts its developers cannot stop and doesn't earn them fees, whereas THORChain operators can act and profit from laundering fees.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella and Jonty
insights.so_what: Regulatory treatment may hinge on control and fee capture.

insights.claim: About 90% of crypto organizations lack anyone who truly understands operational security, because most crypto security researchers are smart-contract auditors rather than traditional cybersecurity professionals.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Opsec talent and services are a structural gap and growth market.

insights.claim: The single most impactful cheap control is deploying EDR (e.g., CrowdStrike, about $150/year per device) on managed devices; many crypto firms skip it for privacy reasons and then lose both privacy and funds.
insights.speaker: Pablo Sabatella (OBSAC founder)
insights.so_what: Endpoint security vendors benefit from crypto's breach wave.

insights.claim: If the industry keeps enabling free laundering, wealth will transfer from retail users to bad actors until they dominate the industry, an existential threat to crypto; enforcement should be industry-led before regulators impose it.
insights.speaker: Jonty (threat intelligence founder)
insights.so_what: Expect growing industry pressure to rethink 'permissionless' norms and freeze/deny service to launderers.
insights.quote: I see this personally as an as a real existential threat to to the cryptocurrency industry.
